utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we notice that Mr. Naletilic is absent. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Naletilic has gone to a doctor for an examination. I believe it is the prison authorities which decided it and I'm sorry that I heard about it today, that is, how he was feeling because he does not wish to tell me about this. He doesn't talk to me about the real state of his health. Yesterday, I was talking with a gentleman and I heard that he can hardly walk, that he has to be carried whenever there is slope, up the stairs, and through the passages, so I don't know what the state of his heart, what his heart condition is. He does not tell me about that because he does not want to -- me to tell you about it because he doesn't want it to interfere with our schedule. But I'm afraid, Your Honours, as I have said a long time ago, that the outcome of it all could be very bad because if he has -- does not have enough strength to go up the stairs, then we know that, and he has four bypasses already and if he wants to survive, he was told a long time ago, that he had to have yet another operation, and pulmonary emphysema which is in a disastrous also state. But Your Honours, I thought -- I've been thinking about it but he did not want me to talk about it and therefore I shouldn't go against his wishes, but I believe that this pace that we have adopted here is another source of trouble. He never wanted to do anything, and of course he signed that we could proceed with the hearings without him and we shall do it always, but I -- this is all that I am at liberty to say now about the present state of his health, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we all wish your client a speedy recovery and we also understand that he waived his right to be present at this trial. Thank you very much. Shall we bring in the witness, please? And Mr. Scott, how long are you going to take this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was going to tell the Chamber that. Once again over the weekend we have -- I have again cut my outline again -- down, both in terms of the questions themselves and in terms of the number of exhibits. My goal, and I do use the word specifically "goal," would be that we hope to finish the cross-examination by the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as we start again today, after the weekend I have a couple of procedural questions I would like to ask you, please. Since you began testifying in this case last Tuesday, have you spoken with anyone about your testimony? Anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except that the relatives called me and I told them how I felt and how my mental state was, I did not talk with anyone else, journalists or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that includes, and not intending to offend anyone, that includes Defence counsel or anyone associated with the Defence teams? You have not spoken to anyone on their behalf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And have you reviewed any documentation, of any documents in any way come to your attention that you reviewed since you began testifying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took along a book which was published publicly. It has to do with the war, because I wanted to remind myself of some events or rather dates, because they necessarily fade with the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I just ask you for the record the name of that publication, the name of the book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The War in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina 1991-1998." Five, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The author's name, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no author. These are articles from the press which have been put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Sir, in connection with the time that you served in various capacities in Bosnia-Herzegovina from about -- during the time approximately 1992 to 1993, you were familiar, were you not, with the concept of the Croat Banovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hrvatska Banovina came into being before World War II, as part of the territorial subdivision of the then Yugoslavia, that is pre-World War II Yugoslavia, and from the earlier instruction in history that I had, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the usher's assistance for the witness to be shown very briefly Exhibit P899, and you can use this one if it's easier, Mr. Usher. Sorry it's not in that particular bundle but you can use this one, please. Sir I'd like you to look at Exhibit P899 for a moment, please, just to orient yourself. Can you tell the Chamber, please, does that map depict an area that sometimes has been called the Croat Banovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even though I'm not an expert in history, but I believe that that is -- that roughly corresponds to the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just as one point of reference, I think my last question on the map, is that that includes, if you will, an extension of territory that goes up as far north from the south as Travnik. If you will, there is a bulge that extends on the map as far north as Travnik. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, in the course of the -- of the war, the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was discussion among the Bosnian Croat side and perhaps also on the Croat side and by that I mean the Republic of Croatia, about some aspirations or goals to once again establish this Croat Banovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this Banovina Hvratska does not include Istra which belonged to Italy or Croatian islands, Cres, Rab, Losinj, and a large chunk of Baranja so that in Croatia nobody would be happy with this because it would mean ceding to Italy the whole of Istra and the number of islands and then ceding Baranja to Serbia, and I think that in Croatia, nobody expected nor talked seriously about the possibility that such subdivision could be the result of any form of political or military activity. However, in different conversations, because there were conversations about everything, the word Banovina would come up but not as a project.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you, or just let me clarify, I didn't mean to suggest to you that the area that -- some of the areas that you mentioned, for instance, Istra would not be part of Croatia. Perhaps you can point out to the Chamber on the map -- well, it's not on the ELMO, but just so that everyone knows what you're talking about. Can you just point out the area you just mentioned that is shown on this map as belonging to Italy, but in reality is part of the present Croatia? Perhaps you can just show the judges that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is today the territory of the Republic of Croatia and with all these islands, the whole Istra belonged to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this part here, this area here did not belong to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir. Apart from those areas, if I can direct your attention very specifically to the area that we were talking about a moment ago, the area, however, that extends if we find Mostar and just roughly looking upward on the map to Travnik. Again that was part, at one time, of -- considered the Croat Banovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not considered as part of Banovina Hrvatska. Under the then subdivision which was very short lived between the Serbian politician Cvetkovic and the Croatian politician Macek, it was the condition for the organisation of Yugoslavia but not Croatia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Again, I'm not suggesting it's part of the state. I think we got into this language issue earlier perhaps with another witness. But the map shows, without talking about the boundaries of the Yugoslavian state, as you indicated a few moments ago, the map indicates an area that's been referred to historically as the Croatian Banovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historically it was called Banovina Hrvatska, Banovina Croatia for a short time before World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Do you recall being interviewed by the BBC at one point and indicating and stating that earlier in the war you decided or you demanded that "Our military goal should be defined at the moment the conflict broke out in Prozor or in Vakuf or in Travnik. We were militarily strong enough to take a territory that could become a Banovina, but we were not allowed to hit first."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend often mentions quotations from some documents. I'd like to ask to see this BBC story so that we can see what it is. Today I shall be showing you some -- we shall -- I will show you some other orders and documents which my learned friend did not show correctly to the Defence, to the Chamber or to the witness because he was in pursuit of an answer that would suit him but then I'll do that when my turn comes. However, when quotations are mentioned, I'd like the witness to be informed about the programme or the text because after all it was many years ago and I believe it is not fair on the witness. He can speak about things like that only if he's shown the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that very regard, I'll ask the technical booth, please, to play the clip that's been marked as P903. And the transcript has been -- should have been distributed about that. It's a very short clip. Your Honours, do you have copies of the short transcript? Has that been provided to you? The video booth, can you hold on for a moment until we make sure that the transcript has been distributed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, does the Defence indeed have to be informed about such a document a minute before the question is asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Prosecution is distributing this document and you'll get one copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we -- there is a matter standing. I'm saying that the Defence is acquainted with the tape and the translation a minute before the examination based on them starts. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the other day we have already made a ruling that you have to show the transcript as well as the tape in the morning, that is, before the cross-examination. I don't think there is anything wrong with the Prosecution on his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, Your Honours, your ruling before the beginning of the cross-examination. This cross-examination has been going on for three days, this is the third day of the cross-examination. And the Prosecutor before the witness was sworn in and it was then that you made the ruling, because the Defence otherwise would have got this videotape and a text had it been to 1.00, now it is it only happens that it is half past 9.00. I'm merely pointing at a possible misuse of law. Your decision was before the witness is sworn in and before the cross-examination, that the defence needs to be handed over all the material. I really do not think it is very just for the Defence to see this tape and the translation just before it is shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as a principle, I quite agree with you that all the materials used before the cross-examination should be furnished to the other part party and to the Chamber. I think this is the principle. However, there are some occasions that -- which was unexpected during the cross-examination because nobody could prejudge the course of the cross-examination, nobody could prejudge how the witness will answer the question. So in exceptions, we allowed this kind of practice during the cross-examination. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think with that, hopefully now everything is in place. Could the video booth please play -- it's a very, very short clip in terms of the relevant part. If the -- if that could be played, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "At the time of the conflict in Prozor or the conflict in Vakuf or the conflict in Travnik we were strong enough militarily at the time to say take a territory that could become a Banovina or some features of that. We were definitely strong enough, but we did not have permission to strike first."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I didn't find out that paragraph on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. President. Mr. President on the transcript that's been marked as P903A it is approximately on the bottom -- about two-thirds down the page or so and you'll see references to Tudjman, Susak and then as you go down a couple of other additional lines on the right side you'll see just to key into the words you'll see the word "Travnik", you'll see the word "Banovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please see the whole tape and could you order the Prosecution to hand over to the Defence the whole tape rather than just sentences taken out of the context? We need to see the whole tape and we believe that the Chamber needs to see the whole tape. Well the Defence will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, do you want to say something? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quite ready to testify as to the authenticity of the tape, the clarity of my words, because they prove precisely that Croatia pursued no military goals, that it did not wish any wars because it says, "If we were strong enough, had we wanted that war, we could have had certain territories, but Croatia or the Croat Defence Council did not want the war, did not start the war," and this tape will show beyond any doubt I said this on the BBC programme, the disintegration of Yugoslavia and I stand by my words. They are accurate, they are precise, and they attest to my thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I believe that Mr. Krsnik's request is legitimate. You have to furnish the transcript as well as the tape to the Defence team, and the -- you may ask some questions concerning with this tape, if there is still some necessary to establish the authenticity of this tape. We may play it from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will provide the full interview to the Defence. I think in terms of authentication, the witness has just very, very clearly said that these were his words and they are accurate. And that's -- I think that aspect speaks -- I think the issue is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My only further question on that, sir, based on what you just said and based on the transcript is, it says, "But we were not allowed to hit first." Who decided or who made the decision, according to you, that you were not allowed to hit first?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision, the decision about that we were not to strike first was taken by the political leadership of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. And even if it were to take such a decision, from the information that I have, I can affirm positively that in that case, the Croatian leadership would have stopped helping in that manner the Croat people and the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, can I just before moving on and that's about to conclude on this topic, but when you say the political leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at that time, can you just name for the Chamber some individuals that you would have included in that leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please, whenever names are mentioned, may we go into private session? I will warn the Chamber after this witness about certain events which require some very serious proportions, however I do not wish to waste time and interrupt the cross-examination about things that happened meanwhile in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina whenever our witnesses are concerned, so whenever names are mention could we please go into private session? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your request is quite legitimate, but on this occasion, I have some hesitations on that because it's a common knowledge of all those persons who are in the leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can go into private session and then I will explain to Your Honours why I'm asking for that, may we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we are back in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct, is it not, that you commanded the HVO forces, the Bosnian Croat armed forces, in the fighting and conflict around Gornji Vakuf in January, February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, once again, Your Honours, I must protest, because I think we're really way beyond the scope of the indictment, challenging the credibility. We did not -- when we cross-examined, we were not allowed to do that, even our examination-in-chief. I think that this -- that this umbrella is simply too broad for this so-called credibility. The credibility can be challenged whilst staying within the scope of the indictment and then it is no wonder that the examination can take a fortnight. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a very limited number of questions on this. One relates directly to the Convicts Battalion. I think it is again fair for the Chamber to hear about this witness's involvement in a number of matters and how it touches on such issues that have come up in his testimony so far. We have tried to get from the witness - I'm going to slow down - as much information as possible about the command structure related to this case, how Tuta fit in the case, or into the HVO, how the Convicts Battalion fit into the HVO, and these questions are related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it can be asked directly without Gornji Vakuf because the Convicts Battalion is not ever mentioned as being in Gornji Vakuf, nor is January, 1991 in the indictment. Nothing of this is in the indictment. Nor is January, February, 1993 in the indictment. They are not in the indictment. So if he wants to know about the military structure, then a direct question may be asked, all about the Convicts Battalion and what its structure can be asked directly, rather than going about events which are not -- with which the accused is not being charged, and I'm sorry he was not charged with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that this issue is related to the military structure of the HVO, which we'll see where the Convicts Battalion will fit in. I will ask the Prosecution to limit his question only concerning with the military structures in this aspect. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm laying the foundation to one or two specific questions to you, but before I do that, I want to you advise the Chamber, if you can and are willing to, you led the Bosnian Croat armed forces in the fighting around Gornji Vakuf in January, February, 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, 1993, there was fighting around Gornji Vakuf, for reasons that I have already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir - and I've indicated to the Chamber that I would try to finish this morning as soon as possible - my question to you is very specifically, and concerning that, you led the Bosnian Croat armed forces, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces of the Bosnian Croats only in an incident in Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993, and only there, only those forces, smaller forces, and for a very limited period of time, then, only in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to ask -- because I'm not exactly sure of the parameters of that answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to Mr. President, I'm going to ask the booth to please now play Exhibit P902, which is another clip from the same BBC interview and the transcripts of that interview have already been distributed, I'm told. If the technical booth could please play the short excerpt, which is P902? The prior one -- I think the prior tape was 903 and this one is 902.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We simply were not able to succeed there for whom there were the Muslim fundamentalists appearing, for whom the Allah and the Koran were sacred, the beginning and the end of the world. All the rest were pagans. All the rest were in fact -- one could already feel that they celebrated Turkey, the janizaries, the conquest, and they were indulging in their dreams about how this all belongs to them, how it is Vakuf and not Uskoplje, that is to say not Croatian but Vakuf, in other words. We reached the point where we could not take it any longer. I led the attack on Vakuf. We seized a sufficiently large part of territory above Vakuf. That is to say we defeated them completely militarily. Then we had to enter Vakuf and there were very many refugees, women, children."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir to make it very clear, then, you led the HVO attack on Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993, as you told the BBC during that interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I led the attack to the confrontation lines which the Muslim forces dug out behind the HVO forces, some 50 metres away from the town, and the lines towards the Serbian territory were some 50 kilometres away from the town. After one month of negotiations with -- in cooperation with the international community, in an attempt for this type of lines to be pushed in towards our back, we only attacked the lines and as was mentioned in that BBC programme, in consultation with Mr. Boban --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I answer in full?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I'm certainly in the Chamber's hands. I think the answer was simply yes. He was in command of the HVO forces and again we can continue on I'll be happy to, but given the amounts of objections and everything else this morning so far, then Your Honour I will not certainly not finish by the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against the Prosecutor proceeding with this cross-examination that has been going on for three days, expecting the answers he can receive, but I would like to indulge Your Honours to allow the witness to explain the answer to the question put to him by the Prosecutor. I think this is the witness's legitimate right. Otherwise we will always have answers hanging in the air and I don't think that this is the purpose of the cross-examination. The purpose probably is for the Tribunal to get a specific and clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the Prosecution asked you a question about whether you lead the attack on that place. I think the first sentence of your answer has already answered this question. If you want to make an explanation on your answer, please do it in a very concise way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a maximally succinct way, Your Honours it was not the attack on Vakuf led which was stated in the programme by the BBC with the very aim of avoiding civil victims or civil casualties, because it is quite clear that at that time already, the HVO, under my leadership in this section, as a civilised army, refused to attack the town and we did not attack the town, we only attacked the confrontation lines. In pure military sense, those lines which were behind us, which were dug out with the purpose of attacking us at a specific moment in time, and at that time, they were not oriented towards the common enemy which was 15 kilometres away from the town. I'm proud with this leadership of the war and in consultation with Mr. Boban, it was decided that we will refrain from doing something which is no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. I must put it to you the Prosecution does not accept all the characterisation of the events but we are not in a position to be able to extend this question and answer further at this time. Now, sir, it's true, is it not, that the Convicts Battalion was involved in the action in Gornji Vakuf and was one of the HVO units coordinated in those actions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, remind me, refresh my memory, but perhaps I just do not understand anything any more. We say one thing. The Prosecution goes on with its own. Let me compose myself. Where does it say that the Convicts Battalion participated in the Gornji Vakuf attacks? If the Prosecution is interested in the military structure of the Convicts Battalion, then it can ask the question very clearly. Why Gornji Vakuf in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- Mr. Krsnik, almost every question you make some objections on it. Some of them are quite legitimate but some of them, I don't believe, is necessary. You have to understand your witness is very capable, very knowledgeable witness. He could deal with all those issues by himself. And Mr. Scott, as we told you a few minutes before, that we are only interested in the military structure and where the Convicts Battalion fit in. You may pursue it along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I ask the record to reflect that the in the morning session, so far, Mr. Krsnik has spoken more than I have in terms of the time that I've been allocated. I want the record to reflect that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask the usher to hand you what's been marked as 221.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again if the English version could please be placed on the ELMO to facilitate the courtroom proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to you look at this document which is a report from an assistant commander named Ivan Kraljevic dated the 18th of January, 1993. I'm going to direct your particular attention to about halfway down the document, the text itself. If you can please find these words, and in the English version it says: "It was reported that two members of the Convicts Battalion were killed in the village of Uzricje" -- forgive my pronunciation -- "today." Now, sir, does that refresh your memory that the Convicts Battalion was involved in the actions in Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I very often refrain myself from raising my opposition, but I would like to know from the Prosecutor what is the base for the raising of this question because this question has nothing to do with the establishment of the military structure. There is no base for either this document or the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I think that the Prosecution want to establish that Convicts Battalion was involved in that action and under the command of the witness at that time. I'm not sure. We have to hear the answer from this witness. Witness, you may answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you precisely ask me what I'm supposed to answer in -- within this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you several times now, but I'll say it again. Do you recall, sir, is it true, that the Convicts Battalion was among the HVO forces that you commanded in the actions around Gornji Vakuf in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question exactly, but it is quite certain that a unit from Siroki Brijeg was there. This unit at that time and this is also mentioned in the BBC programme, where I said that I felt uneasy since the Muslims and the enemy party do not have as many pieces of artillery as we do have, and that a war of that sort is not a good war as far as my ethic feelings are concerned. And Mr. Cikota was up there with a small group of people, a smaller group of people. It was something at the level -- nothing of the kind of a battalion was there. That group of people had between 15 and a maximum of 20 members under the command of Mario Hrkac also called Cikota, also known as Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, they were acting as part of the coordinated HVO forces at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group of people at that time on that line followed my command, my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, in moving forward I'm going to ask the usher's assistance probably going to have to hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I re-sorted the documents, as you may recall for Friday morning, to a smaller bundle, appears that one, I'm sure it was my fault, was omitted and so I'm going to given to the usher now with your permission, Exhibit 230.1, which should have been in the original, thicker bundle, but if he can put the original -- the B/C/S version to the witness and I'll put the English -- you can have my English version although it's the only one I have as well. So I'll have to look at the ELMO myself, I'm afraid. Mr. President and for the Registry's benefit as well, it may be, and I've not had a chance to look further, but it may be that this document was previously marked as 235.1. I'm not saying it has to be resolved this minute, but it may have been called 235.1 it's now 230.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report or an order coming from - I believe the next page would show - Milivoj Petkovic. Let me stop there for one moment, please. In January, 1993, was Milivoj Petkovic your superior, your military superior, for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic at that time was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask to you look at item number 3. Do you recall you wanting or someone, if it wasn't you, either you or someone else wanting Colonel Siljeg to report urgently to Brada in Mostar and send a report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf directly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this text, it is demanded from Geneva where peace negotiations were held, asked by Milivoj Petkovic and not by myself, asking Colonel Siljeg to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, do you have any reason to disagree, sir, that the reference to Mr. Siljeg reporting to Brada, which means beard, does it not, that's the -- referring to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for me to say that in certain moments of time, I had not been called Brada. It is likely that this reference is made to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to go forward, please, to April of 1993. Do you recall, sir, in early April, 1993, on approximately the 2nd of April, 1993, participating in a meeting in Central Bosnia with Valentin Coric, the Tihomir Blaskic, Dario Kordic and others about the current situation in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I have the usher's assistance, please in placing before the witness P272.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, for the record -- I'll wait for those to be put on the ELMO. Sir, for the record, I'm going to indicate to you and for the Chamber that these are minutes of a meeting on the 2nd of April, 1993, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. And as I direct your attention to particular parts of the minutes, I think you will see references to statements attributed to you and I will certainly give you a chance to look at those. Directing your attention to the first -- after all the introductory information, sir, on the English version, it's the part of the page that starts the paragraph starting with the words, "General Praljak." Do you see that it says, "General Praljak opened the meeting by informing those present about the arrival of five or six commissioned officers from Herzegovina. He briefly reported on the signing of the plan and pointed out that UNPROFOR would be staying for another three months. This declaration establishes the immutability of the borders of the Republic of Croatia, no way to change them any more." Now first of all, is this a reference when you say "the plan," is this some plan that was then being discussed in connection with the peace negotiations in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With full respect, Mr. Scott, you can believe me that I would need a lot more time after ten years to bring, to refresh from my memory a -- hundreds of meetings, thousands of meetings we had, neither to you nor to the Tribunal would I want to give no answer. However, I must be sure before answering any question of this sort. I cannot even find the text where this is said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can assist you, sir, if I can. In the first page of the B/C/S version which is a handwritten document, after the -- in the bottom half of the page, the first handwritten B/C/S page, there is a what we would call an asterisk. Do you see there the reference to your name, Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Perhaps we should give the witness some ten minutes or the time during the first break to read the document through because it is a document of five, six, seven pages, and all handwritten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it is very difficult for me to read this. I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in the Chamber's hands if the Chamber wants to take a break early, I'm not opposed to the witness reading it in full if that is what his wishes are, but of course it's up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, are there any documents that you want the witness to read? You might furnish it to this witness altogether so he could make the best time of the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me look, Your Honour, if there is going to be any substantial additional documents of any length. Mr. President, in the few documents that I have remaining for exhibits, I don't think anything else would require any sort of extensive review, with the possible exception of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So we will resume at 20 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, have you had a chance to look at that document now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right. Since you've now had an opportunity to look at the document more fully, are you able to confirm that the Chamber, and of course I don't expect you to have a photographic memory of this meeting some years ago, but can you confirm to the Chamber that you recall attending a meeting such as that in early April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that I was at this meeting in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think the last question that was pending, sir, before the break, was there was a reference -- I read some of the language from the first paragraph of the document to you and there was a reference, for example, to a plan, the signing of the plan. Were you referring to the plan coming out of or resulting from certain peace talks in Geneva around that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This has to do with the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, which was signed in Geneva and apart from some words which I did not understand, and some of my -- some of the sociological objections that I have, everything else agrees with the signed plan of the international community and parties concerned. I only have one comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the first page, here a declaration is mentioned, a declaration, and the immutability of borders. I do not think this has to do -- this applies to the Republic of Croatia. I think it applies to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that the person who wrote this wrote it wrongly, the Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia, by virtue of its recognition, its earlier recognition by the Badinter Commission, had its borders immutable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to spend a lot of time arguing about that, frankly, except to say that admittedly I don't read your language, I apologise, but in the handwritten version of the B/C/S document on the bottom of that first page, it appears to be quite clearly written, the "RH," not the RBIH, but RH. And doesn't that typically stand for the Republic of Croatia, Republika Hrvatska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Letters, yes, but no declaration -- there could be no declaration in April 1993, about the unchangeability, the immutability of borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think this is a mistake because it is completely illogical [as interpreted]. It -- the declaration granted Bosnia and Herzegovina guaranteed borders and the text refers to that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. If I could ask you to turn over to the next page. I'll try to ask you a few additional questions about this document before continuing. I want to you find some language, please, discussing, and just as a point of reference, perhaps you can find the sentence that starts with the words, "The Serbs will be granted large concessions in organising the state. And I believe that there, almost nothing will be left of the state." When you say "almost nothing will be left of the state," are you referring to what was then the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that state, that after being divided up, there would not be much left of it? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that according to the Vance-Owen Plan, the central authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be left with what had been signed then. In my view, that didn't amount to much. But this has to do only with an internationally signed plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I can have your assistance, please, since we are relying primarily on the ELMO for the English version, perhaps you could assist me in following along the right portions of the document. The part we are referring to now would appear in starting at the top of the second page. All right, sir, with that in mind and in light of your answer just now, you then as you just did, stated at the time and have stated again today the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna will remain, it will have its own assembly, and the provincial government will rule the country, the central government will have nothing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where the word "assembly" is or diet is mentioned, I cannot find it anywhere. The government is mentioned but the parliament, the assembly, the diet, are not mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right. I appreciate that, sir. I'm not in a position to argue about the B/C/S language with you. But was it your position and was it recognised at the time that as a result of the plan, as you understood it, not just yourself but Bosnian Croats, essentially the central government in Sarajevo would cease to, as you say here, would have nothing; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Mr. Scott, that under that document, and the international plan, they would get what that international plan said. And it is correct that in this international plan, the central government, because the Serbs were given any concessions, that central government would not be as strong as it is interpreted in the colloquial political sense. The word "nothing" must be the word used at the meeting, but there is no where any mention what is this nothing. So this is the implementation of the international plan. It clearly emerges from the text that we are happy that the plan had been adopted, and of course we are happy because it puts an end to the war. And it is quite clear that we want to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to try very hard to finish your cross-examination in this session. So I am going to ask you to help me in moving forward, please. If I could have -- if you could continue on down the document for some number of lines, and for the English version, Mr. Usher, if you could put the next page, page what would be on the bottom, page 93, on the ELMO, please? At the top part of that page, and I'll ask you, Mr. Praljak, if you can find the language in your version, there are these words, "Talks with the BH Army in Sarajevo about to begin. We shall ask for HVO government in our provinces. Those who choose not to submit themselves to that can leave our territories." Now, sir, do you recall that around this very time, the 1st of April 1993, that Mate Boban issued an ultimatum that the ABiH subordinate itself to the HVO in provinces that were then being referred to as 3, 8 and 10, and if they didn't do that, that come the 15th of April, 1993, the HVO would take matters into its own hands?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, such an ultimatum was never issued. That part which speaks about the reattachment of units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the provinces which according to the Vance-Owen Plan were predominantly Croat, at the same time clearly and unambiguously, speaks about the reattachment of the Croat Defence Council to the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the provinces which were under the predominant Muslim --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, because of the need to move forward, I'm going to suggest to you and I put it to you that in fact there was such a demand and that what you said in this meeting that we referred to a few moments ago was exactly consistent with what Mr. Boban had said. Now, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, Mr. Scott. What would be correct? And Mr. Scott, I will not expedite matters by distorting the truth. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the question has been put to you several times, sir, and I'll move on. Can you please continue on with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher can you please move to the next page? Starting about a fourth of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you find these words, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not sure we are on the same -- if I could -- yes, if it could be moved down a bit, if we could see a little bit more of the top part of the page, please. Thank you very -- bit more, just a bit more down, I think. There, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could find this language it starts "but what will happen if they ask us for other municipalities? Our policy helped to us take everything we could. The negotiations, well, something must be signed." If you see that. In the interest of time, I'm going to skip a few lines, it's there, everyone can see it. And then you come down to the end of that paragraph and it says, "The homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state. It is all as clear as day." Now, when you're referring to "the homogenisation of our population," what did you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant facts, Mr. Scott. The homogenisation is not a project with -- originating -- which originated either with Slobodan Praljak or the Croat Defence Council. The homogenisation came into life as part of the expulsion of the population of the Muslim and Croat ethnicity by the Serbs and also it was due to the departure of some Croats from the territories controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and unfortunately, has been going on and still goes on to this day in Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are de facto --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm going to stop you unless the Chamber instructs me otherwise. I'm going to move on to the next question because you've given your answer. Counsel can ask you other questions about this if he likes. Sir, you said a moment ago this was simply stating a fact but did not reflect your word was, I think, "project". Let me please direct your attention further down the page in a statement that is attributed to you, general, starting with this language: "Territorially". If you could move this up a bit, Mr. Usher, please on the ELMO, just a bit? Thank you. "Territorially speaking, we shall take that and wherever else there is Croatianhood as written. What use is a territory where there are no Croats? We need the territory in the borders that we inhabit." It was the HVO project, was it not, sir, to take the territory where the Croatianness was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the image which the Prosecutor is interpreting by phrasing this question was not and is not all that simple or black and white. It cannot be answered yes or no. So this question and earlier questions - I was patient - however, are questions which are tricky questions because if the witness says yes, then it will be a confirmation after number of statements that the Prosecutor has made. And this question and other questions are actually cuckoos' eggs. The Prosecutor is trying to trip up the witness and I believe the Prosecutor should ask direct questions if he wants direct answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Leading questions by their nature suggest an answer and they include a premise, and that is by the very nature of the question and it is indeed the Prosecution's case and it is indeed what we are suggesting to this witness that contrary to the answer he gave a few moments ago, this document, and the part that I just fairly put to him, it's right in front of him, there is nothing unfair about it, it suggests to him that his own words indicated there was indeed a project to take as much territory as they could for Croatia. I think the question is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the witness. I understand it's a difficult question to you, witness. You may give us an explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, Your Honours, this question is not difficult for me. At that time, the Croats were reduced and this is what this text says, to 11 per cent of the Bosnian and Hercegovinian population and this text refers to the difficult situation, to the predicament that we the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina found ourselves in. And all this text speaks about is the Vance-Owen Plan and within that framework, territories are mentioned, territories which were allotted by this plan. There was no, nor could be, no were we strong enough, nor at the time when we militarily could, and that was clearly said in the BBC's programme too, we did not want to conquer anything down there. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if that is correct, then why is it that on the 15th of April, and the 16th of April, excuse me, 1993, up and down the Lasva Valley and also in Herzegovina a series of HVO offences were launched to enforce the HVO's interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you should indicate the time, the place, the map of offensive actions, and I put it to you that you are interpreting it contrary to the facts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll give you some very specific examples. The HVO attack on Ahmici in which more than 100 civilians were killed on the 16th of April 1993, a factual situation that has been extensively addressed by this institution and those facts have been found in two separates judgments of this court. I point you to the attacks on Sovici Doljani on the 17th of April, the very next day. I put those to you in response to your question, sir, if it was all agreed and if it was in the Vance-Owen Plan and there was nothing more to fight about, why did the HVO launch those attacks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that at the time when certain things were happening, I was not in the territory, but I can give you my view since you are inviting me to do that, Mr. Scott. Both as a Croat and as a member of the HVO, I'm ashamed of what happened in Ahmici. I am not familiar with the situation in Sovici as a whole and I believe it will be established by the Honourable Court at the end of this case. I am referring to the intentions to stop the war and I'm quite confident that throughout the war, our intentions were to stop the conflict, at hundreds of meetings, work in the field, but unfortunately, I do not think that we are to blame that it failed. But even the Vance-Owen Plan was thwarted because Mr. Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature from that plan and as many times after that and before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat Defence Council never withdrew --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead and finish your sentence, sir, never withdrew from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all international talks that were conducted about the fate and internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which the political and military wings of the Croat Defence Council participated, and the leadership of the Republic of Croatia, I do not know of any such plan of the international community which we did not respect fully. When I say we, I mean the HVO, and I can also add the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to -- we have to go forward, I'm sorry, and I can't put any additional questions to you about this topic at this point because we don't have enough time. I would like to direct your attention to the Mostar region, and sir, you were in Mostar during the fighting there on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably in Croatia, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to please hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 380.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to take a look at that document and so that you can see it and so that it's clear, there are two -- what appear to be two related documents here and two translations of the two documents, just so there is no confusion about that. In the handwritten B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read it first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm just trying to assist you so there is no confusion. You can look at either of the two handwritten versions as you wish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, perhaps you could put the English version of the first page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you send this response to a request from Colonel Siljeg making reference and stating approximately the following, "For the time being we are not able to send any soldiers for reinforcement. You are well aware of the situation around Mostar." And were you in Mostar at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, this is not my signature. This is not my handwriting. This is not my style. And this is not my manner. This is a forgery, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, before we leave that, then, and before I accept that, sir, would you look -- the second handwritten document which will be reflected on the second page of the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could put the next page of that version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this document appears to have on it the markings that this was an order being sent from Mostar on the 10th of May, 1993, to the operative zone and to Colonel Siljeg. Now, if we can look --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I sign two identical orders once as Slobodan Praljak and the second time as Brada? These are forgeries, Mr. Scott. This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not suggesting it's necessarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I help Your Honours? These are documents written by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. We could judge what kind of document it is. We just want to hear the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not suggesting necessarily, we can, I suppose dwell on it later if necessary, but I'm not suggesting you necessarily wrote them in your own hand, sir, but I put to you that it would not be unusual, it is not unusual for senior officials of any organisation to have orders issued in their name or prepared for them. I'm not suggesting -- I assume you're not telling us that every single document that you were ever involved in as a senior official or officer that you personally handwrote every order and handwrote every communication and did that yourself. You had aids who assisted you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we hear the origin of this document? Because we do not know from where this is -- is it from Zagreb archives? We have absolutely no information as to where this document -- as for the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, you may furnish this information to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe it comes from the Zagreb archive but I want to qualify that because I don't have it right in front of me, Your Honour, but that's my memory as I stand here and I will confirm it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is also, sir, I should also indicate, a third version which is a typed, electronic -- which looks like, sir, one of the types of electronic communications which you yourself have confirmed were the type sent and which bears the fact and it has a stamp on it indicating that it was in fact communicated. If you can look to the last document, the last page of that document, admittedly the copy is poor, but can you see that, please? Isn't that what a Paket communication looks like?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, this copy is very bad and nothing can be seen from it, but let me repeat that I signed my documents, that the signature cannot be forged, neither in peace and particularly not at wartime, unless some ulterior objectives are thus attempted to be achieved, and that what I have in front of me is a pure forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, well, sir, putting the document to one side and it's the last question I think I'll ask you about this, do you recall, sir, whether you recall the document itself? Do you recall giving an order or making a communication around the 10th of May, 1993, where you communicated to Colonel Siljeg, in reference to the BH Army, quote, "Send them the ultimatum yourselves. If they don't stop, you are free to act as you see fit, pound them with artillery and whatever else you can think of, flatten everything in sight." Now, do you remember giving that order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is not my style, although for the sake of being correct, as far as Your Honours are concerned, in a grave situation during a war, particularly when territories are being lost, when you are defending something, you utter words which beyond and outside that situation, might sound unusual. But these are not my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, but your answer just now you're telling this Chamber you allow for the possibility that on that date, or around that time, you would have given an order to the effect, "Flatten everything in sight"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say this, Mr. Scott. I only said that in a war, at the time of any war, even that war, sometimes orally, in difficult moments, words are spoken for the sake of being aware of what the truth looks like in a war, but let me repeat it for the fifth time, this is not my style, this is not my manner, this is not my handwriting. These documents are forgeries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, in terms of the words, you included then such words as, for instance, "Kill all the civilians in Ahmici," those are the kind of words that can be issued -- stated during a war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refuse to answer this question, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this question. In the firing that took place on the -- in East Mostar during the second half of July, 1993 and continuing into August and thereafter, as the senior HVO commander, overall commander, can you please tell this Chamber what steps if any did you take, if any, to avoid firing on or hitting civilians or civilian objects?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you must be aware of my stand. In Travnik, where I was, in Gornji Vakuf, where I halted the actions, although in a war, soldiers are not allowed to fire from houses in which civilians are located because this is a violation of the customs of war and in this type of situation, wherever I found myself in them, I did my best to do and to try to avoid civilian casualties, even in situations where the enemy defence lines were located in areas which were also areas populated by civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the Prosecutor was asking you a very specific question, the location is in Eastern Mostar, the time is second half of July, 1993 and continuing into the August. It's a specific time period, specific location. You may answer this question within this framework.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never did I give this order, never did I approve it, and for a good period of time, when I was the commander of the HVO, I spent on the confrontation line around Rama and Gornji Vakuf, believing that the Muslim offensive, Neretva '93, which was aiming to the coast line, would be the most fierceful [as interpreted] in this particular territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir is it correct, then, that you will not answer either the president's question or my question specifically with regard to East Mostar, what orders did you give or steps did you take to ensure as much as possible that civilians and civilian objects in East Mostar were mot fired upon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither in writing nor orally have I ever issued such an order, nor have I made it known that anything like that is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's not exactly the answer to the question that I put to you. Not whether it was allowed or not, what steps, what affirmative steps did you take? Can you take us to some orders, tell us some affirmative actions that you took as the senior HVO commander to ensure against, as much as possible, that civilians and civilian objects were not targeted by HVO forces in East Mostar? I put it to you, sir, as a senior commanding officer, it is your responsibility under the laws of war to take such actions. Now tell the Chamber what actions you took.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander, undertakes steps by giving orders. There are no steps, Mr. Scott, which you think may have existed. A commander gives orders. A commander gives instructions to his officers what they may do and what they may not do, and I do not know what steps I could have made beyond this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever punishment -- punish, discipline, withdraw, terminate a subordinate officer for not taking -- firing upon civilians in East Mostar? Was there ever a time? Did you take one disciplinary action against an HVO officer for firing into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Mr. Scott, I put to you that we were not firing at civilians. We were not firing at civilians. Just like the bombs from Eastern Mostar to Western Mostar were not aiming at civilians. The confrontation, the battle line, was in the town, the artillery was located inside the civilian population. The mortars positions were inside the buildings. What happened to us was that our soldiers also fired shots at UNPROFOR and some UNPROFOR members were killed as a result. This resulted by giving an apology to the UNPROFOR, by burying the soldier, and by making attempts to avoid such situations in future. There have been dozens of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall -- do you recall a situation where HVO artillery -- when Muslim civilians would gather, for instance, at water trucks to take water home, the artillery fire was opened on those water trucks while the civilians were gathered there collecting water? Do you recall those situations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott. I cannot either recall this type of situation, nor could they have happened with my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, I'm going to ask that you be shown, please, Exhibit P584.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, if page -- Mr. Usher, if the fourth page of that exhibit in the English could please be put on the ELMO showing the second half of the -- second, the bottom half of page 4 in English on the ELMO, please. Mr. President, I'll just tell the Chamber this is either the last exhibit or next-to-last exhibit that I'll put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember saying to a British battalion liaison officer during the last week of August, 1993, and I refer you, if you can please find the pages, in the English version if you can look to the end of that paragraph comment, did you not tell the British officer -- sorry. At the same interview Mr. Praljak stated that he would have taken Mostar had it not been for the UN delivering aid to the Muslims? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The humanitarian aid to Mostar, as you had an opportunity to see that, contrary to the desires of the people who were expelled and beaten, was delivered by General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I appreciate that fact and we saw you on the -- if it's the same situation, if that's what you're telling us, we did see you on the APC, the armoured personnel carrier. But, sir, you got on that armoured personnel carrier, I submit to you, and I'm not questioning again your personal courage for a moment in this regard, you got on that because of tremendous pressure that came from the political leadership and the Zagreb leadership because there had been such an outrage expressed at the blockade of humanitarian aid. When Zagreb told you to let that humanitarian convoy pass, that's when you took those steps; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I took this step on the basis of my own initiative. At that time, I was not authorised to disperse the population. I had to see to it that the convoy had the necessary security and that the UN soldiers were safe. And this happened. I let tens of convoys through, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you tell the British battalion officer in the last week of August 1993, you would have taken Mostar if it had not been for the UN delivering aid to the Muslims? Is that what you told him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott. I think that this could certainly be a misinterpretation. I did not say anything like that. I particularly did not link the fact of the humanitarian convoys with the military situation, and I do not think that the convoys would help or not, had some plans been made, had some plans been made. And I repeat, that through all my efforts and forces, even against the refugees' will and assuming personal responsibility for personal reasons, I let the humanitarian aid convoys through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, before I leave this topic of Mostar, and turn to the last exhibit and the last questions I'll put to you, I must -- I'm required to put to you, I think, that in connection with your presence in Mostar, at the beginning of the fighting there in May, I must put it to you, sir, that a witness, a public witness, I believe I can -- let me just confirm with Mr. Stringer. Just wanted to confirm that I didn't disclose a name improperly. Excuse me. Sir, a Prosecution witness by the name of Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9674 to 9683. Falk Simang has testified to this Chamber that he saw you, together with Tuta, on the morning of the -- when the attack started in Mostar in May of 1993. What's your response to that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, another misinterpretation. The -- this was not said by Mr. Simang. Rastani were confused with Mostar and to my question, Mr. Simang answered with me, I did it so if evidence is being interpreted, could this be done correctly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, is that the right characterisation of the testimony of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm referring to the transcript pages 3817 to 3820 where the witness said:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see General Praljak in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One morning when we picked up our ribbons. That was these ribbons to recognise we changed these ribbons every morning and when we collected them, that was in a restaurant at Mostar. It was there, when General Tuta and General Praljak and two more people were there." That's the question I put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I simply put it to you, because I think I should give you the opportunity to respond to that again, that a Prosecution witness has identified you as being in Mostar at the beginning of the attack. Now, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I'm sorry, could we stop the cross-examination and let's check the transcript? It was not the 9th of May. It was not the 10th of May. We should know what we are talking about. I insist on a correct cross-examination. What date, what month, was quoted? Is it what I said? Is it the continuation of his testimony? We can't just put it out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was asking the question I thought to give -- out of fairness to the witness to give him an opportunity to respond to that proposition. I will simply to conclude this examination I'll simply go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But first of all, you have to tell us on what date is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The beginning, what Mr. Simang said, Your Honour, was, it was the beginning of the attack on Mostar. That's what he said. And that's in the transcript. That's in the portions that I referred you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Put your question in this way. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what attack? Which attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Two dates are in question. The 9th of May and the 17th of June, and there are other dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us. Witness, you may answer the question put forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in Mostar at that time, in May. I was there when we were defending ourselves in Rastani. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Sir, do you recall an instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. President, this is my final set of questions and I'll have one exhibit about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a time in approximately the middle of June, 1993, where you personally had an encounter with the accused Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, in connection with an incident, some trouble occurred with Tuta's men in the town of Prozor where Tuta's men broke into some Muslim apartments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, another misinterpretation. Who ever mentioned Tuta's people and whoever mentioned Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for instance, perhaps the witness would like to see, Mr. Usher, Exhibit 469.1. Perhaps, Mr. Usher, once again, you could please put the first copy of the English page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I can't read anything here. This is illegible. Your Honours, this cannot be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, it's not my intention, of course, at all to quarrel with the witness but if the Chamber -- I can have the Chamber shown the B/C/S version, and while I agree that one would prefer a better copy, I submit to you that it can be reasonably read, and if need be -- Mr. President, since I can't read it any way, perhaps I can show my -- have my version shown to the Chamber so you can see what I'm talking about. Mr. President, I submit to a native B/C/S reader -- it might be difficult, especially -- more difficult for someone who didn't read the language, but to a native B/C/S reader, that document can be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we will proceed with this document but you have to bear in mind that it's very difficult to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hear the Chamber, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you -- do you recall -- this is a police -- this is a report from the HVO military police in Prozor, titled, for the record, "Report on offences against public law and order by Tuta's men in Rama, Prozor municipality, which occurred on 17 and 18 June, 1993." And I put it to you, sir, that you should indeed remember this incident because didn't you personally have an altercation with Mr. Naletilic in connection with these events?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, believe me, this document can be read out, but cannot be read quickly. Could I be given sometime, please, to read it through so that I can be sure of my answers? Please. Have an understanding for my desire not to answer by heart or to give you a wrong answer, and I simply cannot read this document. It's almost illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may have a few minutes to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while he's doing it, I say this only if it will assist the Chamber. In the original, thicker binder of documents which were provided to the Chamber at the beginning of the cross-examination, if the Chamber were so inclined, you can probably find this exhibit toward the very end of that binder, since I know we haven't been able to look at all of those individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm told -- I was just told by Ms. Fleming that it should be the sixth document from the back of the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you now recall this incident -- these series of incidents, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott. I can recall that subsequently I was informed about the incidents and -- but frankly speaking, I do not know what it was all about and what report of the military police was concerned. And in this context, I cannot give you an answer that I would be able to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance please, directing, in the English version, to the third page of the report, please.
