utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Praljak, if you can please try to find, as best you can, the paragraph -- try to -- it would appear to be on page numbered 2 on the top. I'm referring -- the B/C/S version is numbered on the top. There is the first sheet and then there is page 1 and page 2, and simply by proximity, if you can look up on the page, a couple of paragraphs before the indented -- there are some two paragraphs towards the bottom of that page that have been indented, if you will. If you cast your eyes, please, a couple of paragraphs above that, do you see the reference, it says, "Later, through the invention of Mr. Praljak and Mr. Siljeg, the situation calmed down. According to certain information, there were negative activities in the Rama Brigade by Tuta's men but all of this fortunately passed off without consequences." Now, again, I ask you, does this assist your memory that you personally did intervene in this situation or is the report -- is it your position to this Chamber that the report is simply inaccurate in stating that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I participated so many times in calming incidents down, situations down, that I cannot, with 100 per cent certainty, say either yes or no. This is a military police report which, except in terms of operations, is not subordinate to the headquarters, to the Main Staff. And in connection with this document, one should contact the military police. The military police was parallel to the Main Staff, apart from situations when they were located on the line and when they were given operational orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. In light of your answer, I won't ask additional questions about the document itself. But I'll ask you again, do you recall, in connection with this particular set of incidents, a personal altercation between you and Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't have an altercation with Mr. Naletilic. I would have surely remembered that. And how could I calm it down had I had a personal altercation with him? If I calmed it down, then there was no altercation with him. If I had an altercation with him, then I wouldn't have been the right man to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And final question, sir, did you or anyone under -- subordinate officer to you, did anyone in the HVO command structure take any disciplinary action against Mr. Naletilic or his unit for this attack on the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not within the HVO structure, and the Main Staff and Mr. Petkovic and I later on could not take, nor did we have any reason to take, anything, any steps, against Mr. Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us several times, I believe, in the last several days that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HVO. Are you changing your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But the Convicts Battalion, in the form in which I knew about it, except for the first case I mentioned, and the Orlovac feature, as its commander appeared Mr. Mario Hrkac and Mr. Andabak, and that is also something that I repeated several times. Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not a part of the military structure. Nor do I know him as a commander of this unit in the military part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Just so the record is clear, then - I don't want to sit down without this being clear - you're not disagreeing - you've not changed your answer that the Convicts Battalion by whoever you say it was commanded by, but you confirm again that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HV -- military HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, as for the structure of the HVO, which you showed me, and I drew with a marker where the Convicts Battalion was, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I thank you for your patience. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, because I believe we have to clear up certain matters. It won't take too long Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Distinguished Mr. Praljak, let me ask you about this minutes and that is P -- this alleged meeting in Central Bosnia. Because I still --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, I still do not know where it comes from, who it belongs to. We just received it from our learned friends a few minutes ago. So a document which says, that this is the war diary of Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, and I really don't know where from this document, how did it crop up. It is a meeting in Central Bosnia and it is P272.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could it interpretations or if you remember anything at all, or the meeting was conducted that somebody took down your words as you spoke or was it done later on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I do not think that the minutes were taken right in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But did you sign it or did the participants sign the document to authenticate it as is usually done?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we, I did not sign anything and of course, all sorts of mistakes are possible. The text was not authenticated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you remember your words, and that is page 4 of the Croatian version, second passage, "There will be extremism but realistically speaking, they cannot get ..." I can't read that. Do you know anything about that? Do you remember those words of that intervention that you made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there is no doubt there were extremists in the Bosnian-Hercegovinian war and I believe I am uttering a logical sentence that the extremists will continue existing but, and we believe that after the Vance-Owen Plan and after that we continued believing that, that we believed that the extremists could not overpower those other forces that were not extremists and that wanted both the end of the war and correctly and justly organised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you say here that the conflict between the Muslims and Croats was the aim of KOS? Do you know what KOS is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what KOS is. KOS is the counterintelligence service of the Yugoslav People's Army and I know for certain that they exerted themselves to provoke a war between Croats and Muslims so as to wash their hands of the aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And unfortunately, they succeeded in doing so in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help me? P271, P27.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question is, did the Prosecutor ask you about the supposed, alleged ultimatum issued by Mate Boban on the 2nd of April 1993, to the BH Army and do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we wait for the document or do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can start, begin your answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was no ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: PP, two Ps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Geneva it was agreed so as to prevent further escalation of the conflict between Croats and Muslims and in line with any -- with every military custom, that the units be re-attached to one another without going into their number or their structure or their personnel affairs, so as to avoid disorder and possible lack of -- mistrust of two armed forces. And that is how every -- what every action of the United Nations looks like, and within such action, even the Russian forces in Kosovo are re-attached, placed under the subordination of the joint command while preserving the full autonomy while they are on their own. And this order says another thing, that along side with the reattachment joint staffs will be set up which will, which will be commensurate to the size of the forces which the HVO and the BH Army have on the front lines. But all this was with a view to stopping the war and preventing possible new clashes. That document is crystal clear and it expresses those wishes that I have just told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this joint statement -- are you familiar with this joint statement of Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban of the 2nd of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this statement. And I think that even I participated in drawing it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I'm being warned, Your Honours, I'm referring to this document, PP271.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this statement interpreted as an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Praljak, did you ever?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P274.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't anticipate, given the length of this witness, having any further re-exam, but I do think in the interests of that that it would be fair to put to the witness to make the record clear that concerning this document the evidence in the case is that in fact it was never signed by Mr. Izetbegovic and describe it as a joint statement is not an accurate characterisation of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, shall we stop here and during the break, we will ask you to reorganise your documents order so that you could show to the registry for them to have -- to be prepared for those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will take a very short time. I'm organised. I have all documents here with me, and I handed them over. And I will resume the examination after the break especially view of what the Prosecutor said that Izetbegovic never signed it and unfortunately has also made a statement in writing, but now you will see the Prosecution's exhibit which speaks to the contrary. Thank you. Sorry, I thought that we were having a break. I thought we were about to have a break, and I thought I'd resume after it but it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break. We will rise until 12.30. --- Break taken at 12.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as we are waiting, my colleagues are trying to talk me into -- well they are not really trying to talk me into, but they want me to tell the Court -- perhaps this is not the right time, but we are not feeling well because we are not allowed to come out on to the terrace. We wanted to get some fresh air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I shall repeat, we are all feeling slightly down. We wanted to come out on to the terrace, have a cigarette, breathe some fresh air, but the security stopped us and said that the Defence counsel were not allowed on to the terrace. Are we second rate citizens? Why can't we go out? Why everybody else can? And they told us to clarify -- to clear it up with you. I'm sorry, perhaps this is not the time. Perhaps this is not a question that should be addressed to you, but my colleagues agree here that we should talk to you about this because we are really all feeling pretty poor. Pretty under the weather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think there should be no problem for you to walk out on the terrace unless you don't have your robe on. Anyway I will look into the matter and I'll ask the Registrar to tell us what is the regulation from the security guard. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'd now like to ask the usher document 295, P295. [In English] Please, Mr. Usher, page number 6. Put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I ask you that, let me ask you about the date which is on the joint statement on that document. You have the document there, if you don't remember. But never mind. Never mind. We shall come to that later. The document clearly shows that it was signed on the 2nd of April 1993. This is PP271. We do not have this document in Croatian so that I will try to interpret it. So the European Danish Delegation compiled a report in which they copy the joint statement and say, "The agreement is dated the 2nd of April 1993, signed in Mostar, signed in Mostar, by Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban." Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am positive that such a statement was signed by Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have document PP272 -- no, P272. [In English] Put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. Praljak, if you read this document, of course, I do not know if you are familiar with it, because it's a document of the 2nd of July, 1997 in which Mr. Alija Izetbegovic -- but I mean you can read it yourself, item 1. So item one says, "I did not sign the declaration in question, Izetbegovic Boban, and I was not in Mostar on that day, the 2nd day of April 1993. I do not remember such a declaration being put forward by any side and it is not in any of the documentation in my possession, Alija Izetbegovic, Sarajevo, 22nd of July, 1997, attention, Judge Claud Jorda."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the definition of the chief thesis of this statement in Zagreb both with Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic and it was a joint agreement. In item 4, envisages the establishment of a joint command and I was also scheduled to join it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you become a member of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was envisaged and an agreement had been reached about that. However, it never came true because the Muslim side changed its views so it never came true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Praljak, you were asked about alleged incidents in Tomislavgrad, in Livno, and I go back to the -- your answer during the direct examination. Can you produce a better picture, a better insight, by offering other examples? How did you or somebody else introduce discipline? What did you do to se that the discipline does -- is enforced and that the HVO is properly structured? Do you have any example?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I believe I spoke not about Livno but about Travnik, and Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But do you have some other example?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, there are very many such examples, and believe me, that I could spend days telling the Honourable Court and you and the Prosecution about them. But then they simply cannot be abridged to a size that would -- that is fit for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I'm referring only to the HVO, to the HVO structure, and your role in it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, it happened many times, in conflicts that happened between the HVO and within the HVO, because there were such conflicts, and between the HVO and the Muslim forces. On two occasions I personally stopped clashes in Mostar by crossing to the east bank. I knew those guys and I believe that at that time, many of them trusted me. However, regrettably, for many reasons, the war took its own course and we were increasingly impotent and I was impotent just as well but we have to defend our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, there is a question that I believe needs to be clarified once and for all. I asked you if there were any ranks in the HVO in 1992 and 1993. Do you remember your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranks, army ranks, yes, even though they addressed us using ranks, General Praljak, Colonel so, General so. Those ranks did not exist in the HVO, the HVO was not -- did not have ranks until I believe 1994, and so there were only commanding duties, a commander. There are two command duties, commanding duties, a unit commander, for instance, a company commander, a battalion commander, a brigade commander, and as regards front lines, there is the commander of the operative zone and then with within the operative zone there is the commander of a particular territory of a particular front line, which is placed at his disposal and then there are units which spend those 15 days or so, that is how long a shift lasted, so they are then subordinated to such a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us, how did those men, how did those individuals become commanders, if you know? How could somebody become a commander in the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One became a commander, as often as, not by valour, if somebody was brave. If somebody demonstrated initiative, a strong desire, then he moved up in his career owing to such properties because in a situation when the existence of a people is under threat, the military -- military expertise, military knowledge which is acquired in academies in normal states is made up for simply by the fact that at such a time, one must know. And so one learns quickly and one masters certain military skill very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But who elects those people? Is it soldiers themselves who will elect their commander by simply recognising such a person amongst themselves, as somebody who is brave and who enjoys -- who commands respect? I must tell you that authority can also be interpreted into English as authority so when I say authority in Croatian, I mean somebody who has strength, who commands respect. Or was he elected by somebody else? And incidentally, you can also perhaps tell us how did Mostar come about -- in Mostar, say, 1992, how did they come about? Who set them up? How were they born? Will you explain the Honourable Court? Will you try to paint the picture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Mostar in April 1992, there were nine battalions of the HVO, ex-- based exclusively on neighbourhoods, that is, areas, several streets, or a locality, so neighbourhoods. And the same principle then underlay the organisation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. With me from a former front line in Croatia, from Sunja, seven volunteers arrived with me. And I placed at Muslims' disposal, all of them, all seven of them so that they would learn faster what to my mind one has to learn -- what one had to learn because I knew that the war was arriving there from the Serb side. It was already in full swing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how were they armed? Was it friends from the neighbourhood, friends from the street? You know, I can't lead you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, don't lead me, I'm trying to. When I say neighbourhood, an area or a street, then it seems to me that within it, all is clear. The most courageous in a particular neighbourhood would be elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course it is clear to you, but I'm asking to you to tell it, to explain it to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the weapons arrived in all ways imaginable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know if people bought themselves or smuggled them or sold them individually, procured them individually in -- equally in Bosnia and outside Bosnia, in Europe? Did people who worked in Europe bring them? Will you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can answer your question very peacefully. Now, weapons were smuggled and brought in despite the embargo, which regardless the fact that one respects and abides by the international community's principles, was an unjust measure imposed upon a people that had been attacked without at the same time preventing the aggressor from these attacks. So either the aggressor had to be stopped or the attacked nation had to be allowed to get weapons. Since both the Croats and the Muslims had thousands of people who lived in Germany, in Sweden, in the Netherlands, in France, literally people from all over the world, through money, helped and were smuggling weapons in their passenger cars across the border. Everybody who was willing to sell the weapons was welcome. To my mind, the embargo became less stringent later on. Therefore we able to purchase weapons from some countries, and the weapons were let through by even some authorities, because it was considered wrong for the people to be left without defences and to be killed without the right to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have to answer my first question. Were the commanders elected or chosen from among the soldiers or were they appointed by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I answer that they were selected from among the people, the strongest and the most courageous, then I answered sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to pursue. I just want to go on to an order which the learned friend mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to offer at this point another clarification. About a year ago, I think it was about a year ago, I don't know exactly when, we brought in the 17 binders and the filings included an order, Defence Exhibit number -- Exhibit 564.1. The document, Your Honours, it is an order dated August 12, 1993. In the course of the cross-examination, Mr. Branica was focusing upon it and you will note that on the first page, at the bottom, it says, "End of document." Nothing follows. No seal. No signature. Nothing. During the cross-examination, however, page 6 was attached to this very same order, although it had been said before that nothing else was contained in this document, and on this page 6, which had -- sorry, corrects himself, the Defence Council, page 2 had been added, although in the course of the cross-examination it was said that there was no second page. On this second page, there is in print written, "Signature, Mr. Praljak," not signed by Mr. Praljak. And this has nothing to do with the order that had been issued by Mr. Praljak a year ago and Mr. Praljak contested it. In this exhibit, 564.1, it says, at the end of the first page, "End of document." Sorry, it is Exhibit 563, Exhibit 563, it says, "End of document," no seal, no signature. We can put all these documents on to the ELMO. In the course of the cross-examination, Exhibit P564 contains a page for which it had been claimed by the learned friend that this is part of the same order, although a year ago, he said that there was no second page to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, maybe you can give some information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Mr. President I can not give any response to any of these matters in a vacuum at all. Are these questions for the witness? Why are we doing this while the witness is sitting here unless there is a question for the witness. I'll be happy to examine these matters, but this doesn't sound like questions for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we can come back to this issue while we are admitting the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to help me. Exhibit 564.1, please. Could you bring it? I apologise. Do you need any help? It's Exhibit 564.1 from the binder with the title, "Praljak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The only reason I was asking is that sometimes you refer to a document 563 and then 564. There are two documents. Okay. That clears it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to explain it. I don't know if I've succeeded. So the document 563 had been submitted us a year ago and now we are referring to document 564.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, would you be kind enough to study this document thoroughly once again? First question, Mr. Praljak, would you please check page 2, paragraph 6 or 7? Is this usually a part of each command -- order, if you are familiar with that, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not. This was not contained in each order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Could you tell me now, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could anybody at any time sign on your behalf without your approval?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody during the war was allowed to sign an order in any form on my behalf. A war is a very serious, very painful, and a very responsible matter. Nothing like that is allowed. Everybody must sign their own orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you have ever had an assistant, an aide?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the HVO, nor in the Croatian Army, did we have aides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. And now let's proceed to the last order. This is document P558.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting let me put this question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The order which the learned friend used trying to say that it was an order for the alleged attack, is this an order part of the combat readiness which was usually referred to or was this an order which was specifically requested from you? I think it is the order of August the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher, would you help me, please? [In English] Because of the time. We have English version and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, this is what I mean by reorganising your documents because it's very difficult to find those documents in those binders so maybe during the break if you want to use any documents, you had better provide with the Registrar a list of these documents so they could have it prepared before we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received these documents today, that is, on Friday, from one binder, about Mr. Praljak, which we had received a few days ago. I thought we had them on hand. I apologise, but I'm just following the learned friend's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this is a daily, regular order made in a war to put the troops in the state of full combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any war, in any army, or armed forces, this type of orders are issued almost every day or it is very rarely that whenever information has been received about possible activity to be launched by the enemy, not to prepare an order on the basis of the intelligence service information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, from where was it -- the order sent and what is the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was sent from the Main Staff, HVO Main Staff, on July 28th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who were the addressees of the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operational Zone Southeast Herzegovina all brigades of the Operational Zone Southeast Herzegovina and the Operational Zone North-west Herzegovina. By the way, I did not sign this order. But in military terms, it is a logical one, and it's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the length, to put it that way, of the battle line when you arrived there and took over the command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO at that time had about 2.000 kilometres of front line, with the Serbian army and with the Muslims living in all the enclaves, if we add up all these front lines, they extended over more than 2.000 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The learned friend in his question mentioned that in Bosnia, the HVO units attacked Mostar. Is this true, or do you have a counterclaim, if it is not true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the Croats and the units of the HVO in central Bosnia was such that in comparison with the number of Muslim units in the Tuzla basin, in the Zenica basin, and in other towns, was such that it is simply logically impossible to assume that somebody would be foolish enough to attack an enemy which has ten-fold number or units, even though this were a part of the political decision, as has often been alleged here. All HVO brigades that were in Sarajevo -- in Stup, in Tuzla, Sol, then in Zenica, by then had been disbanded by the BIH army, with more or less casualties, but I still owe Their Honours and the learned friend, Mr. Scott, an answer to the question, who were the casualties when the incident had happened which we have seen in the videotape that you had shown to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the Defence counsel asked you about very specific question, that is the HVO units attacked Mostar. Concentrate your answer on that particular location. I mean you have to answer this question whether the HVO attacked Mostar or not. This is a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know what was the translation, because I cannot follow the translation, the transcript. But my question was whether it is true that the HVO started the attacks following the learned friend's claim in Central Bosnia, but not just in Mostar. I didn't limit myself to Mostar only. I don't know how this was translated, but the witness certainly can answer your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were attacked, the HVO was attacked. The enclaves which were there were shrinking. They were exposed to ever-fiercer strikes, and at the expense of very severe combat, they managed to survive, not all of them, not Vares, not Vojno, not Bugojno, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Konjic, Jablanica, the Neretva valley, who attacked whom there, if you have any knowledge of that? And what do you personally know, what crimes were then perpetrated in the Croatian enclaves, if you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, two objections, one is with all respect, and allowing for my long cross-examination certainly, but with all respect, I don't think the purpose of re-direct is to cover the same ground that was covered on direct examination, number 1. Secondly, to the extent that calls for an answer about involving tu quoque, we again object as all ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, the purpose of re-examination is not to give you another chance for your direct examination. I think in this aspect, your question should concentrate on challenging or reputing any cross-examination put forward by the Prosecution. Secondly, Mr. Krsnik, we are not interested in who attacked whom during this conflict. We understand that all sides did some terrible things to each other. That's not the subject matter of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. You know that in the indictment, it is alleged that the HVO on the 16th of April, attacked and the learned friend in cross-examination tried to confirm this allegation, so I just wanted to have the witness confirm whether this is true. When the Prosecutor asked about a crime which has nothing to do with this indictment, my question was to the witness, whether the Defence submission that the HVO did not attack, that the ABiH attacked all territories inhabited by the Croatian Army, and I don't know from whom they were defending them, under the disguise of defence. In fact, I am continuing with the submissions made in the course of the cross-examination by the learned friend today. I know that I speak fast and I can't change, but when I mentioned the Croatian Army, what I had in mind was the HVO. I apologise. I cannot concentrate at all time and sometimes I fail to mention the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say Croatian, sorry, Your Honours, when I say the Croatian army, I would like to make it clear that from this point onward, I am referring to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have heard a lot about the issue, who attacked whom, and we know that terrible incidents happened during that period. So you may skip that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours, I'll skip it but unfortunately it seems to me neither the public opinion knows it nor have they been charged by this Tribunal, but I will certainly skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is my last question, Mr. Praljak. The situation in Mostar when you were there, the Prosecutor put to you questions about the alleged shellings. How frequently was, to your knowledge, Western Mostar shelled and whether the targets were selected or were shellings from the eastern to the western bank made by chance without any plan? Was this a typical house-to-house combat situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A typical house-to-house combat. The front line is located inside the town. It is my submission that both sides were firing equally at one another. It is my submission that our side never wanted to target civilians, but it is quite undisputed that this could have happened. And it is my submission that on the right bank of the Neretva, in the part of the town under HVO authority, there were at all times, at least 8.000 Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Final question: How often did the shelling happen by the ABiH of Western Mostar and where did the bombs land?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, how frequently? That's difficult to answer. But let me repeat, that I spent quite some time in Rama and Gornji Vakuf but this was frequent. It was frequent, the town was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Thank you very much for your patience and thank you for coming. This is the end of my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, only three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, generally speaking, if you did not make the direct examination, you are not allowed to cross, to re-examine this witness. But as you said at the very beginning to us, this witness is your common witness, and Mr. Krsnik took the words from your mouth. I mean he asked the questions you wanted to ask. So in this circumstances, I will allow you to do your re-examination. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, during the cross-examination the question of your rank arose, of your rank in the Croatian Army, the Croat Defence Council or today. When did your active duty -- when your active duty stops, are you entitled to your rank nevertheless? And are you still addressed as "general"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war ended, I retired. One can write in the public only a retired general. And the use of all the other things, uniform, when one says general, that is all regulated by the rules of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will omit one question and shall move on to the next one. Do you know that in the strategy and tactics of warfare, there are also legitimate combats under urban conditions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are legitimate military actions in urban conditions, and it is thought that under wartime conditions, civilians living in urban centres, in the streets of which there is fighting, are, in the zone of combat and therefore they are responsible for their own fate. Example: When General McArthur in World War II was taking Manila, he proclaimed the city an open city. The troops surrendered and the civilians are then protected by the law of war, under those conditions. If the civilians are in the same area and the same buildings are in the proximity of buildings where the fighting is going on, then it is impossible to separate military action from possible civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Clark? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: General Praljak, I have a few questions for you. I'm going back to the early days of the independence of the Republic Croatia and you told us about your background at university and then your position as a director in the Croatian television making documentaries, I think, you said, and films. And then you explained to us that any right-thinking member of Croatian society would obviously rush to the defence of their fatherland when it was being attacked and so you came to be in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Clark, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I stand corrected. I'm just giving a brief synopsis of some of what you said. And you explained then how although you had no military training but you had done a lot of reading, you came to be a highly positioned member of the Croatian Army. Now, was the Croatian Army at that stage made up of a core of people who had -- who had been used to responsibility like you but with no military background but also a hard core of soldiers who had been properly trained and who had come from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a television director. I worked in the theatre. I did some documentaries. The majority of people, but we have to have the time frame. In 1991, in 1991, the majority of people on the ground were volunteers and the majority of them had not passed any officer training, but when called upon by president Franjo Tudjman, then many Croats, officers in the Yugoslav People's Army quit the Yugoslav People's Army. General Tus, General Stipetic, General Agotic and they then took over all the responsibilities, all the business dealing with the restructuring of the army. They did more that kind of job than organising the defence lines on the ground. So they were by and large in staffs, in headquarters rather than on the ground. I went in my civilian clothes as a foot soldier, fully aware, and I would like to repeat this once again, and no matter how long it may take, because I wanted to live in freedom. And I'd like to repeat another war, if only it would make me feel as a free man. I had no dilemmas about that and I believe the same applies to a large part of the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm talking, Mr. Praljak, about the Croatian Republic only and the difficulties with the Serbian aggression. We are not talking about Bosnia and Hercegovina at this stage. Did you -- starting off as a foot soldier, I take it you very rapidly became a general in Croatia. Did -- who appointed you as a general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I went to the area of Sisak and after three months or so, together with a very well known director in the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Medjumorec and a well-known actor, Sven Lastor, we were invited to President Tudjman's and he asked us to accept ranks. Truth to tell, I said "Well, I'd rather not have a rank." I said, "I'd rather only keep the title of a commander of something." But Mr. President, at that time, affirmed that the army had to have ranks, that it had to be structured, more with every day, and that would be -- would we be so kind as to assume such a responsibility? So there was no reason for to us say no. And I honourably assumed my first rank and I still feel honourable with this rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have to say it was the faster rise than most people are used to. Did you, Mr. Praljak, while you spent the little time, the three months, obviously becoming acquainted with soldiering, did you at any stage learn anything about the rules of war, the Geneva Conventions, the conventions of war, or was this something that you knew about from reading and as an educated man?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already knew it all, Your Honour. I knew it all. And I never missed in Sunja or later, I never allowed that anywhere in my vicinity or in the area covered by my power that something happens that would run contrary to all the rules of warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You also explained to us, Mr. Praljak, a few days ago, and I think I might even have asked you some questions at that stage about how in the early days of the war, that with the best intentions of the commander, like you, to prevent any atrocities, if you had no police structure or no discipline with newly formed troops to prevent any possible atrocities in 1992, I think you were talking about, an incident outside Mostar, when you seized control of a Serb installation. Now, what I want to ask you, Mr. Praljak, is did the army progress between 1992 and 1993, to a better formed, trained and disciplined army, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Now, we've moved stations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia, the situation became much easier because there was a part of the state which could function as a state. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was much more difficult. Your Honours, to man 2.000 kilometre long front lines under normal wartime conditions would require 2 million men, 2 million soldiers, and we have 400.000 inhabitants. As regards the structuring of the army of the HVO, we were successful as between April until autumn, 1992, both in terms of structure, discipline and various other terms, because there was still a forceful hope that the war would be resolved quickly. International forces arrived and the peoples who lived down there and especially among Croats, strongly believed that the west would bring a fair peace to those lands. When I say the west, I mean through their political and military intervention. Regrettably towards the end of 1992, as I have already said, the Muslim approach to the political organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina changed, the Vance-Owen Plan fell through and the success then began to decrease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak we are moving away from what I'm really asking you. What I want to know is that by mid-1993, had the army of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, become used to the concept of military discipline and the application of the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The troops were acquainted with orders and decisions of the government, I mean the decisions of the HVO government, and in that respect, the facts are very clear, but in 1993, because of the major war effort, the structure, the structuring was worse than in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So is what you're saying, Mr. Praljak, is that after the conflicts became interCroat and Muslim, discipline broke down, that enmity was such that the rules of war might have been forgotten?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The expelled -- the vast number of dead, a disproportionately large number of dead for such a small population, entailed all that -- I mean everybody who has watched any war knows what kind of a chaos is created. I do not say that a crime can be justified by another crime, but it is an undisputed fact that a crime produces a crime. And that it is very, very difficult to stop. Unless one has a global solution to the problem and unfortunately that was lacking until Srebrenica and Dayton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I want to move from that, then, Mr. Praljak, if I may, to another aspect of the HVO. Do I understand you correctly that this is an organisation that had a political wing and a military wing and that whereas you were the Chief of Staff of the military wing, you obviously were subservient to the political wing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first there was the Ministry of Defence, and as the -- and Mr. Mate Boban was the commander above the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Would you have been aware, Mr. Praljak, that Mr. Boban went on a fairly regular basis to report on the conduct of the war to Zagreb, to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that and I knew about that. I knew that not only Mr. Boban but I with almost all the Muslim commanders, with Mr. Boban, with Mr. Izetbegovic, believe me, there were dozens of meetings, and always we would have to start the same story from the beginning, how to stop, how to put an end, and unfortunately, it all depended on the political solution, which was not being offered, that is the parties remained on the opposed sides and of course the Serbs also wanted their share in all this, and that is how it went on and on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I don't want to you misunderstand my question. I was specifically referring to Mr. Boban and others from the HVO government, the political wing of it, going regularly to Mr. Tudjman to report on the conduct and progress of the war and not the negotiations. Were you aware that this was happening? I'm not talking about negotiations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam, we did not submit reports on the progress of war because after all one could hear it in the news, in all the news. There were no military secrets there. But neither did the Muslim nor the Croat part of Bosnia can do anything or do anything without going through the Republic of Croatia, be it weapons or clothing or bread or flour or milk. Nothing at all. So there were talks about how to do that, and that happened from one day to the other, because in war, everything is possible, but no military reports. Yes, there may have been conversations about it, but nothing in the form of reports, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you quite a lot of questions, on another aspect but before we come to that, there was a question that was put to you by Mr. Scott that interested me. Your answer interested me. You were asked about the leadership of the KB on a number of occasions and you said that after a particular event, where you shared command with Mr. Naletilic, that as far as you were aware, Mr. Andabak was the leader of the KB, the Convicts Battalion. When Mr. Scott pressed you at a later stage about the fact that Mr. Naletilic was the leader of the Convicts Battalion, and that has been the Prosecution case, you answered, and I took a note of it, you said that in the form that you knew the Convicts Battalion, the commander was Andabak. You didn't know of Mr. Naletilic being the commander of this group in the military part. Now, two parts of that response make me believe that you perceived the Convicts Battalion as having a military aspect and a political aspect. And that's the answer -- that's how I interpreted your answer. Do you have any comment to make on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering with full confidence, Your Honour. This battalion had absolutely no political say, no political influence, in any matter, but Mr. Andabak, Mr. Mario Hrkac, Cikota, at whose funeral I attended because he was a very valiant soldier appeared as commanders. And Mr. Tuta only when I mentioned him not that he spoke there, he simply commanded authority. He commanded respect. In 1992 May, place, Orlovac, I described that exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason that Mr. Scott I'm sure is putting these questions and I'm putting the questions is that we have a wealth of documents which indicate that the commander of the KB was Mr. Mladen Naletilic, but you say in the form that you knew it, it was Mr. Andabak who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you must have read Churchill's statement that one lies so much in wartime as much as in hunting and before the elections, you know this war was replete with lies about events, about persons, about meanings. Everybody wanted to be bigger, larger, more important. I am saying what I think is the truth, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I want to ask you, Mr. Praljak, about the system of signing orders. I believe you told us that there were no two nights that is you spent in the same bed during the period that you were Chief of Staff in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does that mean that you had no headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did have our headquarters, Your Honour. During that period of time, when I was the commander, the headquarters was in Citluk, in Herzegovina, near Medjugorje, but at that time, the most intensive Muslim offensive was about to start. And much more important was to be on the ground, and one simply had to be on the ground because the units were in a very difficult situation, completely exhausted, and the command, as one thinks, one ought to comment in French or American army, that did not exist. Mr. Tole stayed down there, around Mostar, in Citluk Mr. Petkovic went to enclaves in central Bosnia, and I, I went to the area around Rama and Gornji Vakuf and I spent much more time on the front line with soldiers than in offices or in a good bed. That is a problem which will arise -- I mean in the contents of notions when we speak about army command, the general, battalion, very little of what one usually means by these terms in normal armies existed over there. I had to be on the front line daily. I had to run from one position to another, to boost the morale and at long last, we managed to stop this very forceful, I repeat, offensive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, led by their commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So you spent most of your time around Rama and Gornji Vakuf. So what happened when you had to issue an order? Did you have a secretariat? Did you have somebody to type out? Did you have a collection of note paper with you? How did you effect the distribution and the bringing into existence of an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three of us, Tole, Petkovic, myself, we all enjoyed the autonomy of command. I do not know what general command could I have signed then. There was nothing like it then. It was the fighting every day, very hard, and orders usually referred to very narrow pieces of territory, that is the front has been broken through, this or that, the orders referred to smaller units, to smaller segments of the front line. I do not think that it was possible to sign a single general order because the situation varied from one area to another, except that we were always defending ourselves, and such an order would have served no purpose either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have denied the validity of a number of orders and in fact, alleged that some of them are forgeries, so what I want to know, and this is an important part of your evidence to clarify for me and the Bench, is if you wanted to issue an order and you were in Gornji Vakuf or another town near the front, how would you get it typed up? And how would you distribute it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have signed such an order because there would be its original and then the Paket Communication would be used to be sent to Central Bosnia or to Citluk or I'd take my car and go to Citluk and sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You still haven't explained to me, Mr. Praljak how it would be typed up. Did you have a secretariat? Did you have a soldier whose job it was to take care of documents and did he follow you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd find always somebody, usually a female person, who knew how to type and then it would be dictated to her. You know, there were some ladies in our army too. They would either be with the medical service or in the kitchen or typing and so I would dictate it to her, sign it and then the Paket Communication was used to send to either General Petkovic or to Zarko Tole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Excuse me for two minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question I really I'm leading to or the series of questions is that armies seem to be like civil servants. Is that -- and bureaucracy, a copy is kept of everything and there would be one filed in headquarters, one sent to the various recipients and one sent for archives. What was the system that you either introduced or inherited with the HVO in relation to the retention and archiving of reports and orders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days of the war, in Croatia and in Bosnian Croatia and in the Croatian Army in which I was and in the HVO, this -- in the early days, depended on how well the commander himself was organised. And in the early days, very little was put down on paper, very few things were filed. Later on, even in the Ministry of Defence, I invested effort, I mean the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, I started working towards collecting as much documentation as possible and then later on in the HVO we endeavoured to record to file and to store. They were officers made responsible for it in the headquarters, and then I do not know where it ended up in the Ministry of Defence or rather the Department of Defence of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But was there a system that you knew of that documents which were emanated from your particular office or any command would be retained, filed and sent to the Ministry of Defence for archiving?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Believe me, I never tackled this problem. I didn't consider it important, nor did I have time for it, for me at that time, I was left with no energy or strength to even ask that question now that I think back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If, as Chief of Staff an order had to be made in an area of the war which was a distance from you and we've heard from other witnesses how travel was difficult, the terrain was difficult, the war was fragmented and travelling wasn't easy. It was also very mountainous, we believe. How would you be able to give an order when you had been told, I take it, by telephone or otherwise, that something had happened in another area and it required direction or an order from you? How would you issue an order in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by and large, under such circumstances, I would hear it over the phone, or we'd have a conversation, and then I'd give some general instructions, and they were always the same practically, "Defend it. Don't give in, forcefully." You know, wartime words. We must -- and then the commander of that unit would issue operative orders, where should, which unit, but I repeat, Your Honour, more -- much more, 80 per cent of what happened happened, both good and bad things, happened beyond and outside any orders, so if there was a strong feeling that one wanted to defend something, then no order could prevent or change the image. We didn't have even the embryo of what is normally called a state organisation, state apparatus, to have a decision implemented, let alone prevent a violation, and that is why an individual played a major role, his resoluteness, the determination, the respect, the will. It is difficult to say that there were the embryos, the germ of organisation in spite of the will to organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: One final question for you, Mr. Praljak. You've had a long day. Did you ever receive, as Chief of Staff, did you ever receive reports from the military police about any of their concerns about what was happening in the area? Or did you receive any reports from the military police at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. The military police did not submit reports to the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council. May I give a broader answer to this question? In the beginning, while still in Croatia, when we talked if the military police should be subordinated to the army, as is customary in normal armies, then the problem arose that considering the very underdeveloped structure it might happen that a commander could also become a dictator, and thus rule the military police too, to make charges and to impose his will. And it was then decided that it would be more democratic even if perhaps less organisationally good, if in parallel with the army a military police were set up, a military police that would not be accountable to the Main Staff and the chief of the army, unless he requested that the unit, because of the bad situation on the front line, be sent to the front line. But he could not make any personnel changes, call to account, or and the Main Staff couldn't -- and outside the operative deployment, the Main Staff had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You didn't quite answer the question that I was putting. Did you personally -- there was the question that Mr. Scott posed to you about a particular incident but I'm just asking you, did you ever receive reports in relation to what the military police were reporting was happening on the ground, especially in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have asked for a report to be submitted to me but I did not receive them on a regular basis, nor were they obliged to send them to me. I could just give them a ring to ask what was going on, what happened, what I was hearing about, but not as a part of the structured communication, but rather my private right to put a question to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak, I'm sure the other judges have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could sit here a little bit longer. Yes, Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Praljak, I should like to hear from you some explanations and clarifications concerning your military situation, as a regular officer of the HVO -- sorry, of the HV, of the Croatian Army, that is, to leave your positions and to go to Bosnia as you have explained it to us, you needed a clear, specific invitation. Were you put at their disposal to travel to the area which your forces usually were not stationed at, or would you be made available to do that, which would mean that your original forces would be able to follow your activities, or would you simply be issued an allowance to take a leave or would you just leave without any particular approval?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, we can imagine that there is Yugoslavia without any citizenship, neither Croatian nor Bosnian and Hercegovinian, because there is no such state. Through the attack on Croatia, in the Croatian Army, we would have many troops who come from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were -- are both Croats and Muslims. Through the attack of the Serbian army upon Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards the end of March, the then chief command -- chief in command of the Croatian Army, General Tus, T-u-s, issued a decree ordering that all those who might, tomorrow, become citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina - at that time it was not certain whose citizens they are - can leave the Croatian Army to fight in the territory of the then-unrecognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the meantime, their families would receive some payment for that, because if this had not been done, had the families of those who went to fight were not taken care of, then we would have been doing something very ugly. Throughout that period, it was not known what is state sovereignty, whether through the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia must dismiss those people from its ranks who came from Bosnia-Herzegovina or give them citizenship or whatever. This is the situation in which, on a voluntary basis, I myself, as well as many others, for reasons that I have mentioned before, decided to go down there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In April, 1992, at Siroki Brijeg, in Citluk, in Capljina, people called you "commander." Did you have any patches, any insignia as commander? Or perhaps some people called you "general." I'd like to know what kind of insignia did you wear? Were they the HV insignia or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I have allowed myself -- well, it may have happened, when I arrived there quickly, to have an HV insignia, but I always had the HVO insignia, without any general's insignia. Well, they could be there as well. You know, I didn't always have two uniforms, Your Honour. So most frequently, there were no insignia on my uniform, the uniform would just be provided for me. But the problem had always been that since I'm very tall, it was very difficult to locate a uniform that I could fit into. So I did not have the HV insignia, although it may be that sometimes when I couldn't change, they were on, but not as an official sign of HV but rather because of technical reasons, I wasn't able to change into something else. They called me "general" because that meant a high degree of safety to the people. You know, in people -- in -- at a wartime, people sometimes put additional feathers on, to be thus given more significance, a sort of a metaphysics of humans' existence. This was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not satisfied with this answer but I will move on. You spoke about the liberation of hills around Mostar in May, 1992, with Mr. Naletilic. Did Mr. Naletilic take part in this liberation and in what capacity? And this was the liberation from whom, from which force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the mountains above Mostar, at that time, there was the corps commanded -- the corps of the JNA commanded by General Perisic, and the Chetniks were also there. Mr. Naletilic -- I described it very exactly, earlier, also, what was his participation and his role. He was standing there with me, and together with him, we were following the evolution of the action, which had been very precisely explained before, by Mr. Andabak and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in what -- he was beside you, but you told us he was not an HVO member. So what was his capacity? Could anybody go with you to the front line and sit next to you and participate in the liberation of a hill?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was very precise in saying that he had certain authority, and that in that sense, he would not -- could not be described as a man on the street. I cannot answer more than that, apart from the fact that he invited me there, that we talked, that the commander explained to me the situation and the manner in which the action was carried out, and that he personally, in a manner which I had described, participated in this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. But with your education and your familiarity with the laws of war, what could you do to protect Muslim civilians from their expulsion? And I -- for instance, [redacted] [redacted] who at that time, a high official of -- Croatian official, who testified here under protection, said that he was helped by Mate Boban. Were you kept abreast of the situation? What could you do to help in such situations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did everything a human being can do. The HVO was the military wing of the army of a people who were defending themselves against a major aggression first launched by the Chetniks and then by the Muslims. 99.99 per cent of my activities were aimed at defending the defence lines. Like in civilian society, when criminal -- when somebody is murdered in either New York or in Amsterdam, when something like that happens, there are procedures, the procedure of finding, identifying and punishing the perpetrator, and I don't think that the mayor of the Hague can be asked on a daily basis what he or she had done in order to prevent the crime that had taken place in his or her city on that very night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't have any questions. I almost never have any questions after Your Honours. I merely wanted to redact the transcript. The last name is mentioned and a witness could be identified through it, so that is my only suggestion that a name be stricken off. Thank you. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that that name will be redacted in the transcript. Thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to help us. We appreciate that very much. We have kept you for a long time here and we all wish you a good trip back to your home town. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Scott. Thank you, the Defence counsel. I hope that I was not too much of a bother. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Krsnik? We have received a list of the Defence exhibits tendered through the witness dated the 3rd April, 2002. We just want to know whether there is any new documents you want to add to this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this should be necessary. I'll check it and I'll do it tomorrow morning. For the time being, I have no new documents apart from the list you have already received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, we also received your exhibits for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I wonder whether those documents are all the documents that you have the intention to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, because we narrowed our examination several times, all the exhibits were not used, and I was trying to -- while I listened to Mr. Praljak in the last hour or so, I tried to limit -- or excuse me, to list the ones that we used. Unfortunately, I noticed when I came back from the last break I didn't bring part of my materials with me, and I apologise. I can give the Court a partial listing now, but I'm afraid to -- for the first day of my examination on Thursday, I'll have to supplement that. But we actually used, as I recall from my records, 587 -- and these will not be in numerical order because they are in the same order they were in in the binder --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Scott, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, could I suggest that you submit new lists tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that we could know which documents have been admitted and which are not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree that would be the better way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that at this stage we are not in a position to admit all those documents, so we have to keep a correct record of all those documents because of the translation issues. We have asked the Registrar to look into this matter as soon as possible, to find a way out for that, but at this moment, we could only have the list of those documents that both parties want to tender. Are there any issues? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like -- I would like to ask for this list of cross-examination exhibits to be also submitted to the Defence so that we can check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my colleague has just reminded me that I should tell Your Honours that we had these documents translated -- put them in translation in November last year, and not in March of this year. We had put them into the translation process at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We already asked the Registrar to look into this matter. Having said that, we will rise until tomorrow morning at 9.00.
